items.content_excerpt: Market Recap for Tuesday, October 13 Small dip on the surface, but real pain underneath though. $DJI -0.35% (51,670) Nasdaq -0.15% $QQQ S&P 500 flat (-0.02%) $SPY What happened?! Chip selloff again: Reports that China's CXMT made big progress on memory chips hit the sector. $MU -5.5%, $AMD -3.3%. South Korea's Kospi dropped 5.5%. Mixed bank earnings: Goldman Sach’s was strong, Wells Fargo, on the other hand, disappointing. Healthcare dragged: J&J down ~5.7%. Rising energy costs ahead of this week's CPI report. 56% of US stocks closed red, even with the S&P basically flat. Rough times. On the bright side from a bigger picture, AI has carried this market all year. When chips wobble, everything feels it. CPI is the next big moment. Let’s hope inflation doesn’t come in too hot. 🥵 Have a goodnight y’all!

items.title: $TSLA Vehicles sit in core goods and the fuel that moves them sits in energy, which means a single purchase gets split across the two halves
items.content_excerpt: $TSLA Vehicles sit in core goods and the fuel that moves them sits in energy, which means a single purchase gets split across the two halves of the inflation report. Core inflation covers the 79.9% of the basket that is neither food nor fuel, and it ran 2.4% in August. Headline, which includes the fuel, ran 3.4%. The gap between them was almost entirely energy. Full explainer, plain English: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=le-mFDuzQd8 Written version: https://techdamentals.com/newsletter/why-cpi-and-core-inflation-tell-different-stories?ref=st Educational, not advice.

items.title: $AMZN Shipping cost is where energy enters the part of the inflation basket that supposedly excludes energy. Core inflation covers the 79.9%
items.content_excerpt: $AMZN Shipping cost is where energy enters the part of the inflation basket that supposedly excludes energy. Core inflation covers the 79.9% of spending that is neither food nor fuel. But diesel moves freight, and freight is inside the price of nearly every physical good. That is the honest weakness of core as a measure. Stripping fuel out of the calculation does not strip it out of the economy. Full explainer, plain English: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=le-mFDuzQd8 Written version: https://techdamentals.com/newsletter/why-cpi-and-core-inflation-tell-different-stories?ref=st Educational, not advice.

Speaking on the Cheeky Pint podcast with AI chief Alexandr Wang, Zuckerberg recalled asking whether the massive spending plan would actually work. Wang acknowledged that success was far from guaranteed, while CFO Susan Li repeatedly warned about the enormous cost of failure. The comments highlight Meta’s challenge in convincing investors that its aggressive AI spending will generate sufficient revenue and profits. The company is investing hundreds of billions of dollars in data centers, computing infrastructure, and advanced AI models to compete with Alphabet, OpenAI, and Anthropic. items.title: Broadcom CEO Hock Tan sparked market turmoil after comparing many artificial-intelligence investors to casino “gamblers” during the DBS Asia
items.content_excerpt: Broadcom CEO Hock Tan sparked market turmoil after comparing many artificial-intelligence investors to casino “gamblers” during the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore. His remarks, reported by Bloomberg, were cited as a factor behind semiconductor stocks’ declines on Monday and Tuesday, as investors debated whether they signaled caution about the sustainability of the AI investment boom. The comments created uncertainty over whether Tan was expressing skepticism toward AI valuations and speculative investment or simply warning that investors are taking excessive risks. Despite the market reaction, Broadcom shares rose 0.73% on Tuesday, while the semiconductor ETF SOXX fell 0.17%, ASML declined 1.86% and TSMC gained 0.17%. The episode highlights the market’s sensitivity to comments from major semiconductor executives as investors assess whether massive AI infrastructure spending can generate sustainable returns. $AVGO $SOXX

items.title: $SOFI A digital bank meets the deposit question in its sharpest form. Net interest income, the gap between what a bank collects from borrowe
items.content_excerpt: $SOFI A digital bank meets the deposit question in its sharpest form. Net interest income, the gap between what a bank collects from borrowers and pays savers, widens early in a rate cycle because loan rates reprice faster than deposit rates. It narrows later, when savers notice what their cash could earn elsewhere. A customer who opened an account on a phone can move money to a higher yield on the same phone. Deposits that move in one tap are an advantage when rates fall and a cost when they rise. Full explainer, plain English: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlan3N9D9mU Educational, not advice.

The short interest was lower and the share price higher. Now that the short interest has risen and the share price has declined. A big enough catalyst on the right day could really get this moving up. That said, not all catalyst are created equal. It would probably take an announcement with dollars attached to it. Something that materially changes forward revenue guidance. Maybe an international revenue stream opening up and expanding TAM. Maybe a large business customer utilizing SofiUSD. I hope any news is released early in the week and not on a Friday. The options market smothers this on Fridays.

items.title: $BLK Asset managers and banks both feel a rate move, through completely different channels. A manager earns a fee calculated on the value of
items.content_excerpt: $BLK Asset managers and banks both feel a rate move, through completely different channels. A manager earns a fee calculated on the value of the assets it oversees. Rising rates cut the value of the bonds inside those assets, so the base the fee is charged on shrinks even when nothing goes wrong operationally. A bank earns a spread between borrowing and lending, and holds the risk of what sits on its own balance sheet. One large firm reported assets under supervision at a record $4.1 trillion this week, which cuts against the simple version of this story. Full explainer, plain English: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlan3N9D9mU Educational, not advice.

items.title: BlackRock upgraded U.S. Treasuries to overweight, ending a nearly six-year underweight position, as 10-year yields climbed about 110 basis p
items.content_excerpt: BlackRock upgraded U.S. Treasuries to overweight, ending a nearly six-year underweight position, as 10-year yields climbed about 110 basis points this year to roughly 5.25%, their highest levels in decades. The firm favors short-term government debt while moving long-term Treasuries to neutral, arguing that higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations have driven the selloff. BlackRock believes markets are overstating future Fed tightening and estimates current yields provide a 75-basis-point buffer against further rate increases over the next 12 months before total returns turn negative. To fund the shift, BlackRock cut U.S. equities from overweight to neutral and reduced agency mortgage-backed securities exposure. Despite the tactical caution, it maintains a structural preference for AI-focused stocks, listed infrastructure and emerging-market equities. $BLK

Boeing’s revenue grows faster than the defense group over the next five years — roughly eight and a half to nine percent a year, taking it from about ninety-eight billion in twenty twenty-six to around one hundred forty-six billion by twenty thirty. The defense names run four to six percent: Lockheed about four and a half, Northrop five and a half, RTX six, General Dynamics four. The earnings picture flips. Boeing’s EPS goes from a loss of about a dollar in twenty twenty-six to roughly fourteen fifty by twenty thirty — a ninety-plus percent annualized rate, but that’s a recovery from a depressed base, not steady compounding. The defense group grows earnings eight to ten percent a year from already-profitable levels: Lockheed from about thirty dollars to forty, Northrop twenty-nine to thirty-seven fifty, RTX seven twenty-five to ten fifty, GD seventeen to twenty-two seventy. So the market’s pricing Boeing as the higher-growth, higher-risk story — faster revenue, faster earnings, but with execution risk baked in . Trying to make investors embrace the longer term . $TSLA Vehicles sit in core goods and the fuel that moves them sits in energy, which means a single purchase gets split across the two halves of the inflation report. Core inflation covers the 79.9% of the basket that is neither food nor fuel, and it ran 2.4% in August. Headline, which includes the fuel, ran 3.4%. The gap between them was almost entirely energy. Full explainer, plain English: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=le-mFDuzQd8 Written version: https://techdamentals.com/newsletter/why-cpi-and-core-inflation-tell-different-stories?ref=st Educational, not advice.

$SOFI A digital bank meets the deposit question in its sharpest form. Net interest income, the gap between what a bank collects from borrowers and pays savers, widens early in a rate cycle because loan rates reprice faster than deposit rates. It narrows later, when savers notice what their cash could earn elsewhere. A customer who opened an account on a phone can move money to a higher yield on the same phone. Deposits that move in one tap are an advantage when rates fall and a cost when they rise. Full explainer, plain English: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlan3N9D9mU Educational, not advice.

The firm favors short-term government debt while moving long-term Treasuries to neutral, arguing that higher real interest rates rather than inflation expectations have driven the selloff. BlackRock believes markets are overstating future Fed tightening and estimates current yields provide a 75-basis-point buffer against further rate increases over the next 12 months before total returns turn negative. To fund the shift, BlackRock cut U.S. equities from overweight to neutral and reduced agency mortgage-backed securities exposure.
